text_blocks.snippet: Generally, you cannot withdraw from your pension before the minimum pension age, which is currently 55, and will be 57 from April 2028, unless you meet specific conditions like severe ill-health or certain job types. Even then, it's usually subject to penalties and taxes. You should check your specific pension plan details for specific rules and options.

list.title: Minimum Pension Age:
list.snippet: The earliest you can access your pension is typically 55, but this is increasing to 57 from April 2028.

list.title: Early Withdrawal:
list.snippet: You may be able to withdraw earlier if you have a severe health condition or if your pension provider allows for an earlier protected retirement age.

list.title: Tax Implications:
list.snippet: Early withdrawals typically come with penalties and taxes, such as a 10% early distribution tax if you're under 59 1/2, in addition to income taxes.

list.title: Hardship Withdrawals:
list.snippet: Some plans allow hardship withdrawals for specific financial needs like medical bills, foreclosure prevention, or funeral expenses, but these are usually limited to the amount needed to cover the hardship.

list.title: Defined Contribution vs. Defined Benefit:
list.snippet: Defined contribution plans (like 401(k)s) generally offer more flexibility in accessing funds, while defined benefit plans (traditional pensions) may have stricter rules.

list.title: Pension Type:
list.snippet: Different types of pensions (e.g., workplace, personal, state) have different rules and withdrawal options.

list.title: Pension Provider:
list.snippet: Your specific pension provider will have the most accurate information about your plan's rules and options.

list.title: Financial Advisor:
list.snippet: Consulting a financial advisor can help you understand the implications of withdrawing from your pension and make informed decisions.
